lane.name: Slacker, jangle, and power-pop revival
lane.definition: 2010s–2020s guitar pop descended from Pavement, GBV, Flying Nun and Big Star: jangle, fuzz, conversational lyrics, short songs, DIY release culture.

albums.label: Gulcher Records
albums.description: Vile's debut is a hazy, homespun collection of fingerpicked drones and mumbled melodies recorded largely at home. It set the template for his sleepy-eyed guitar style before Matador came calling, for listeners who want the slacker-rock revival at its most unpolished origin point.
albums.lineage: Grew out of the Philadelphia scene around the War on Drugs, which Vile co-founded; its haze sounds like a direct precursor to the countrygaze and slacker records of the 2010s.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: Vile's Matador debut adds full-band muscle and squalling guitar solos to his stoned drawl, making it one of the most rock-and-roll records in his catalog. The driving opener 'Hunchback' shows him leaning into Crazy Horse-style fuzz. It's the record where the War on Drugs alum became a solo guitar hero in his own right.
albums.lineage: Signing to Matador connected Vile's Philly lo-fi scene to the wider indie-rock world, and its sound looks ahead to the 2010s slacker and jangle revival.

albums.album: God Is Saying This to You...
albums.label: Mexican Summer
albums.description: A compilation of early home-recorded tracks that bridges Constant Hitmaker and his Matador debut, showing the same murmured vocals and unhurried acoustic-electric picking before a full band thickened his sound. It's a stopgap for completists tracing his rise from bedroom tapes to indie stardom.
albums.lineage: Part of the same lo-fi Philadelphia tape underground that produced Constant Hitmaker; a bridge into the more full-band Matador era.

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: A hazy, reverb-soaked debut about suburban New Jersey boredom, built on interlocking clean-toned guitar lines and unhurried tempos. A foundational record for the 2010s jangle revival.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Flying Nun/Feelies-style jangle guitar pop; a key node connecting classic jangle to the 2010s slacker/jangle scene.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Another early self-recorded Bandcamp album from Alex G's prolific pre-label period, built from warbling home-studio pop songs and pitched vocal manipulation. The songwriting is skeletal and the fidelity is intentionally rough, but melodic hooks poke through the murk. It's for listeners tracing the earliest roots of his songwriting before Domino signed him.
albums.lineage: Shares the same DIY home-recording aesthetic as Winner, part of the flood of Bandcamp full-lengths that built his cult following before DSU broke through.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: One of Alex Giannascoli's earliest self-released Bandcamp full-lengths, built from home recordings with warped, pitch-shifted vocals and drum-machine loops. It's rougher and stranger than the records that made him famous but already shows his knack for a warped melodic hook, for deep-catalog listeners.
albums.lineage: Part of the early-2010s Bandcamp lo-fi boom, the self-released run that fed directly into DSU and the rest of his catalog.

albums.label: Chapter Music
albums.description: The Melbourne band's debut is loose, plainspoken jangle-pop full of local color and wry deadpan vocals. Drawled, small-town observations sit over relaxed, chiming guitars, a key early record of the 2010s Australian slacker-pop scene.
albums.lineage: Sounds descended from Flying Nun jangle, by way of Melbourne's Chapter Music scene.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: A quieter, more assured record than its predecessor, built on fingerpicked acoustic figures and Vile's half-asleep drawl, this is often cited as his creative breakthrough. It slows the tempos down and lets the songwriting carry the weight rather than the guitar pyrotechnics. It's the album that turned casual fans into believers ahead of his commercial peak.
albums.lineage: Refines the Crazy Horse-and-folk hybrid of Childish Prodigy into the more meditative style that would define his Wakin on a Pretty Daze and B'lieve I'm Goin Down eras.

albums.label: Play Pinball!
albums.description: Parquet Courts' scrappy, self-released debut, full of talky, deadpan vocals and loose, Pavement-indebted guitar interplay recorded on the cheap.
albums.lineage: A direct extension of Pavement's slacker guitar-pop songwriting into a Brooklyn DIY setting.

albums.label: Domino
albums.description: A cleaner, more melodic refinement of the band's suburban jangle-pop sound. Warm, mid-tempo guitar interplay sits under gentle, nostalgic lyrics, for listeners who like their indie rock hazy and summery.
albums.lineage: Continues Real Estate's jangle catalog, which sounds indebted to Flying Nun and the Feelies.

albums.label: Chapter Music
albums.description: A hazy, unhurried debut of ramshackle jangle-pop from Melbourne, indebted to the Flying Nun and Feelies sound. The vocals are offhand and half-mumbled, for listeners who like their guitar pop loose and sunlit.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Flying Nun jangle-pop and the Go-Betweens/Clean lineage; part of the same 2010s Australian guitar-pop wave as Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever and The Goon Sax.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A collection of short, murky home recordings that lean further into the pitched-vocal manipulation and tape-hiss atmosphere that became his early trademark. Songs blur together into a woozy, half-remembered whole rather than standing as individual singles. It's a transitional record for fans tracking his path toward DSU's breakout.
albums.lineage: Sits in the same self-released Bandcamp run as Winner and Race, the DIY foundation that eventually caught Orchid Tapes' and then Domino's attention.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: The last of Alex G's run of purely self-released Bandcamp full-lengths before signing to Orchid Tapes, still built on lo-fi four-track pop songs with warped, childlike vocals. Melodically it's a bit more confident than Rules, hinting at the songwriting leap DSU would make. It's for listeners who want the full arc of his self-taught bedroom period.
albums.lineage: Closes out the self-released Bandcamp era that set up his signing to Orchid Tapes for DSU and eventually Domino Recording Co.

albums.label: Captured Tracks
albums.description: DeMarco's Captured Tracks debut coined the woozy, chorus-pedal 'jizz jazz' sound that defined blog-era slacker rock: loose, warbly guitar lines, half-mumbled vocals and a stoned, unhurried tempo throughout. It set the template for a decade of goofball-slacker singer-songwriters.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Pavement's shambling guitar pop and Flying Nun-style DIY jangle; its own influence on the 2010s slacker-rock and bedroom-pop wave that followed is well established.

albums.label: What's Your Rupture?
albums.description: The breakout record: rambling, funny, deadpan talk-singing over tight guitar interplay that recalls Pavement and the Modern Lovers. It is half stream-of-consciousness and half punk energy, with songs like 'Stoned and Starving' stretching into wiry jams.
albums.lineage: Sounds like the clearest 2010s inheritor of Pavement's slacker guitar-pop songwriting.

albums.label: Salinas Records
albums.description: Allison Crutchfield and Kyle Gilbride's band debuts with scrappy, fuzzed-out guitar-pop that splits the difference between 90s indie rock and Philly basement-punk. Direct, unpolished and hook-driven.
albums.lineage: Grows out of the same Philadelphia DIY scene as Waxahatchee and Radiator Hospital, with a guitar-pop sound that seems indebted to Pavement and GBV.

albums.label: Don Giovanni
albums.description: Katie Crutchfield's bedroom-recorded debut, written and tracked in a week at her family home, is just acoustic guitar and a cracked, plainspoken voice working through devastation and longing. It is the rawest end of the slacker/DIY spectrum this lane covers, closer to a diary than a studio record.
albums.lineage: Grows out of the DIY punk and cassette/Bandcamp network Crutchfield came up in, and sounds indebted to the deadpan funny-sad songwriting line; it seeds her entire catalog, including her later, more country-leaning work covered elsewhere in this atlas.

albums.album: The Double EP: A Sea of Split Peas
albums.label: Marathon Artists
albums.description: A compilation pairing Barnett's first two self-released EPs, introducing her rambling, deadpan talk-singing and wry observational lyrics to an international audience for the first time. The guitar tone is loose and unpolished, closer to garage rock than the more produced records that followed. It's the release that put her on critics' radars before her proper debut LP.
albums.lineage: Grows out of Melbourne's DIY scene and Barnett's own Milk! Records label, the base for the deadpan Australian songwriting wave around her.

albums.label: Chapter Music
albums.description: This second Dick Diver LP is loose, warm and conversational, built on ringing guitars and half-sung, half-spoken vocals in the vein of the Go-Betweens and the Clean. It's a high point of the early-2010s Melbourne jangle-pop revival, for fans who want the sound that shaped a wave of Australian slacker-pop bands.
albums.lineage: Grew out of Melbourne's Chapter Music scene alongside Boomgates and Twerps; its sound feels like a template for later Melbourne jangle bands such as Chook Race.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: Vile's fifth album stretches sun-baked slacker rock into sprawling, double-LP length, blending gorgeous fingerpicking with heavy guitar drift. The mood is unhurried and half-stoned, closer to a daydream than a statement. It is the record where his Pavement/Crazy Horse-indebted sound became widescreen.
albums.lineage: Vile was a founding member of The War on Drugs in Philadelphia; his sound here seems descended from Pavement's loose-limbed guitar rock and Neil Young's amp-drone side.

albums.label: Salinas Records
albums.description: Sam Cook-Parrott's project delivers scrappy, hissy, hook-filled songs with a plainspoken, earnest voice at the center. It is unpretentious DIY power-pop-punk in the classic Philly basement mold.
albums.lineage: Part of the same Philadelphia DIY network as Swearin' and Waxahatchee, with a lo-fi guitar-pop sound that recalls Guided by Voices.

albums.label: Carpark
albums.description: Sadie Dupuis's knotty, GBV/Pavement-indebted guitar riffs collide with tossed-off, sardonic lyrics across a record that swings between melody and noise. A key 2010s document of the slacker-noise-rock crossover.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Guided by Voices/Pavement's loud-quiet guitar-pop songwriting.

albums.label: Salinas Records
albums.description: A noisier, more layered second record, with dual songwriters Allison Crutchfield and Kyle Gilbride trading lead vocals. Dense, fuzzed guitar interplay drives short, urgent songs built for basement shows.
albums.lineage: Continues Swearin's Philadelphia DIY guitar-pop songwriting, which sounds indebted to Pavement and GBV.

albums.label: Autumn Tone
albums.description: Twin Peaks' scrappy debut is all ragged garage-jangle riffs and teenage swagger. Short, shouted songs and loose, bashing drums capture a young Chicago band playing fast and not overthinking it.
albums.lineage: Rooted in Chicago's teenage DIY scene, with a sound that recalls garage rock and Pavement-style slacker guitar-pop.

albums.label: Don Giovanni
albums.description: Recorded at home with Swearin's Kyle Gilbride, this is a fuller-sounding but still homemade record about family, addiction and young adulthood in Alabama. The song-to-song shift between fragile acoustic pieces and full-band fuzz set the template for a decade of Waxahatchee records.
albums.lineage: Extends American Weekend's DIY lo-fi songwriting with Swearin'-band muscle; a key transitional record between bedroom-pop slacker rock and Crutchfield's later, more countryish songwriting.

albums.label: Orchid Tapes
albums.description: Alex G's breakthrough, a warm and melodic leap from his earlier tapes released by Orchid Tapes, mixing pitch-shifted vocals with genuinely gorgeous pop songwriting. It's still lo-fi but far more melodically assured than his self-released run. It's the record most people point to as his arrival as a songwriter to watch.
albums.lineage: The culmination of his self-released Bandcamp period, and the record that plugged him into the Orchid Tapes/bedroom-pop scene before Domino signed him.

albums.label: Captured Tracks
albums.description: DeMarco's best-known record is a warmer, more melodic take on his slacker sound, about the anxieties of encroaching adulthood delivered with a shrug. The title track and 'Passing Out Pieces' became blog-rock standards.
albums.lineage: Refines the '2' blueprint into DeMarco's signature sound; a touchstone for the 2010s jangle/slacker revival.

albums.label: Manic Static
albums.description: A kinetic Chicago DIY debut mixing jangly, interlocking guitar lines with garage-rock urgency. It is the first half of a strong two-album run, for listeners who like their jangle fast and loud.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Flying Nun/Feelies jangle crossed with garage-rock energy, rooted in Chicago's DIY venue scene.

albums.label: You've Changed Records
albums.description: Nigel Chapman's conversational, half-spoken vocals ride over loose, unhurried jangle-rock guitar, closer to Jonathan Richman or Silver Jews than most of their slacker-rock peers. Bookish, philosophical lyrics over simple, warm arrangements.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to the deadpan funny-sad songwriting line (Silver Jews/Drag City) crossed with VU-style jangle guitar; the start of one of the decade's most consistent guitar-rock runs.

albums.label: Salinas Records
albums.description: A denser, more collaborative record built on Cook-Parrott's plainspoken, hook-first songwriting. Short, bright pop-punk songs about love and small humiliations fly by, for fans of basement-show intimacy.
albums.lineage: Continues Radiator Hospital's lo-fi pop-punk songwriting within the Philadelphia DIY scene, with a sound that recalls Guided by Voices.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Released while the band was still called Sports, this self-released debut is scrappy, hooky basement pop-punk. Fast, fuzzy guitars and wry, confessional lyrics set up everything the band would polish later.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to GBV/Pavement guitar-pop songwriting by way of the East Coast DIY scene.

albums.label: Electric Muse
albums.description: A Busan band's debut full-length, applying warm, ringing jangle-pop guitar tones to plainspoken, sea-town songwriting. It is the start of a consistently pristine throwback indie-rock run, understated and melodic.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Flying Nun/Byrds-style jangle-pop, transplanted to the Korean indie scene.

albums.label: Grand Jury Music
albums.description: A tighter, more craft-oriented second LP that mixes ragged jangle-pop with rowdy garage energy. Multiple singer-songwriters trade short, catchy songs, making it the band's most instantly fun record.
albums.lineage: Continuation of Twin Peaks' garage-jangle songwriting, moving toward wider recognition.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Warehouse's self-released debut is a kinetic, interlocking-guitar record fronted by Elaine Edenfield's commanding, sing-shouted vocals. It sits closer to Sonic Youth's angularity than to straightforward jangle-pop, but is still built on tightly wound guitar jams, for fans of wiry post-punk.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Sonic Youth's interlocking-guitar vocabulary, part of the Atlanta post-punk/jangle underground.

albums.label: Domino Recording Co.
albums.description: Alex G's Domino debut pushes his warped pop songs into stranger, more processed territory, with pitch-bent vocals sitting alongside skeletal drum machines and unsettling interludes. It's a deliberately harder listen than DSU, trading immediacy for atmosphere. It's for fans who like the unease under his prettiest melodies.
albums.lineage: First release for Domino after his Bandcamp/Orchid Tapes run, expanding his cult audience while keeping the same bedroom-pop DNA.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: Will Toledo's Matador debut re-records and remasters highlights from his sprawling self-released Bandcamp catalog, bringing his hyper-verbal, deadpan songwriting to a wider audience for the first time. It's noisier and more chaotic than his later full-band records. It's for fans curious how his bedroom-era songs sounded once given an actual budget.
albums.lineage: Bridges Toledo's run of self-released Bandcamp albums with the full-band Matador era that produced Teens of Denial and beyond.
key_tracks: Bad Role Models, Good I Am

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A tightly recorded set of plainspoken, jangling Melbourne guitar pop, in the same scene as Dick Diver. Deadpan vocals and short songs keep it brisk and unfussy.
albums.lineage: Sounds descended from Flying Nun jangle, within Melbourne's jangle-pop scene.

albums.album: Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit
albums.label: Milk! Records
albums.description: Barnett's debut is a wry, rambling slacker-rock landmark, its deadpan run-on lyrics detailing house-hunting anxiety ('Depreston') and open-mic dread ('Pedestrian at Best'). Loose, twangy guitars and a conversational drawl carry the songs.
albums.lineage: Sounds heir to Pavement's talky slacker rock, alongside Australian jangle peers like Dick Diver.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: A more introspective turn with banjo and piano alongside the guitars, led by the single 'Pretty Pimpin'. Vile's cracked, mumbling delivery and stream-of-consciousness lyrics stay pure slacker even as the arrangements soften toward folk.
albums.lineage: Sounds akin to the Pavement-to-Silver Jews thread of deadpan funny-sad songwriting, in a more folk-inflected register.

albums.label: Father/Daughter Records
albums.description: Remember Sports' second album and first for Father/Daughter tightens the basement pop-punk of their Kenyon College beginnings into brisk, hook-first songs. Carmen Perry's elastic voice leads scrappy, fast guitar-pop that suits fans of loose, energetic DIY indie rock.
albums.lineage: The scrappy basement pop-punk starting point of Remember Sports' own arc, which grows toward the more collaborative, fuller songwriting of Slow Buzz and Like a Stone.
key_tracks: Getting On in Spite of You

albums.label: Carpark
albums.description: A more confident, bigger-sounding follow-up, with Dupuis's guitar leads pushed further forward and her lyrics turning more pointed and political. Still rooted in the band's angular, GBV-descended riffing.
albums.lineage: Continuation of Speedy Ortiz's Pavement/GBV-indebted noise-pop songwriting.

albums.label: Chapter Music
albums.description: A more polished, dreamier follow-up, with brighter production but the same loose jangle songwriting at its core. Male and female vocals trade off over chiming guitars, keeping the debut's casual charm.
albums.lineage: Continues Twerps' jangle-pop, which sounds indebted to Flying Nun and the Go-Betweens.

albums.label: Merge
albums.description: Waxahatchee's Merge debut loosens the structure further, mixing drum machines and organ drones into the guitar songs for a woozier, more experimental slacker record. It is the least polished-sounding of her Merge albums and the closest to classic 90s indie rock.
albums.lineage: Bridges Cerulean Salt's basement sound with a more expansive, era-blurring indie rock palette; part of the same Merge-era run that established Crutchfield as an indie rock and later Americana songwriter.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: Will Toledo's first full-band studio album turns Bandcamp-honed bedroom pop into classic-rock-scaled narrative rock, nodding to the Cars, Pavement and Jonathan Richman. It is a sprawling, self-lacerating song cycle of long, anthemic, funny-sad songs.
albums.lineage: Toledo self-released many albums on Bandcamp before signing to Matador; the result sounds fused with Pavement's slacker irony.

albums.label: Buzz Records
albums.description: Casper Skulls' debut EP introduces the Toronto band's dual-vocal, college-rock-indebted guitar pop, drawing on Pavement and R.E.M.-style jangle with conversational, story-driven lyrics. It's shorter and scrappier than their later full-lengths but sets the band's voice from the start. It's for fans who want the earliest version of their sound.
albums.lineage: Part of Toronto's Buzz Records jangle-pop roster alongside acts like Weaves; a direct forerunner to Mercy Works and Knows No Kindness.

albums.label: Trouble in Mind Records
albums.description: A shambling, K Records-worthy set of hooky, unhurried indie pop from this Melbourne trio, all ringing guitars and plainspoken vocals over loping tempos. It's cheap, cheerful, and unfussy in a way that recalls the DIY jangle-pop of decades past. It's for fans of Flying Nun-descended guitar pop with an Australian slacker drawl.
albums.lineage: Part of the Melbourne DIY jangle-pop scene that also produced Dick Diver and Terry, distributed internationally by the American slacker-rock label Trouble in Mind.

albums.label: Lame-O Records
albums.description: Matt Scottoline's Hurry plays tight, hook-forward power pop with an easy, unfussy jangle and plainspoken lyrics about heartbreak and self-doubt. The songs are short, sunny-sounding and quietly anxious underneath. It is for listeners who like their guitar pop clean and catchy.
albums.lineage: Part of Philadelphia's Lame-O Records power-pop circle; the sound is indebted to Big Star and Superchunk.

albums.label: Good Cheer Records
albums.description: Mo Troper's scrappy, hook-crammed debut packs GBV-scaled power pop into a lo-fi, fast-moving set, full of pop-culture non-sequiturs delivered with a snotty, deadpan sneer. Songs rush by on buzzing guitars and sticky melodies, for fans of four-track power pop with attitude.
albums.lineage: Sounds squarely indebted to the Guided by Voices four-track power-pop tradition, filtered through the 2010s Portland DIY scene.

albums.label: Paradise of Bachelors
albums.description: A more assured, road-tested version of the band's talky jangle-rock, with Chapman's lyrics turning toward philosophy and self-doubt over bright, ringing guitar lines. Songs like 'Stargazer' stretch out patiently, for listeners who like their indie rock literate and unhurried.
albums.lineage: Continues the band's jangle songwriting, which sounds indebted to Silver Jews and the Velvet Underground.

albums.label: Ivy League Records
albums.description: The Melbourne five-piece's debut EP sets out the template their albums would follow: three guitarists trading tightly interlocked jangling lines over driving, motorik rhythms. It's unpretentious, sun-bleached guitar pop that announced the band before Hope Downs.
albums.lineage: Grows out of the Go-Betweens/Triffids strand of Australian jangle-pop filtered through a more driving, Feelies-like guitar interplay.

albums.label: Upset The Rhythm
albums.description: A Melbourne group with members of Total Control and UV Race debuts with wiry, deadpan guitar-pop songs about everyday minutiae. It sounds closer to a shaggier Flying Nun update than to noise rock, for fans of dry humor and trebly guitars.
albums.lineage: Grows out of Melbourne's DIY jangle/post-punk scene and sounds related to the same Australian guitar-pop wave as Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever and Twerps.

albums.label: Slumberland Records
albums.description: Molina strips away Dissed and Dismissed's crunchy guitar for mostly acoustic, Bee Gees- and Byrds-indebted miniatures that rarely stretch past a couple of minutes. It's a hardcore lifer distilling pop songcraft into brief, gutting fragments.
albums.lineage: A quieter turn from the Weezer/Teenage Fanclub-sounding power pop of Dissed and Dismissed toward the acoustic Big Star and Byrds side of the same lineage.

albums.label: Grand Jury Records
albums.description: A big step up for the band, with keyboards and horns thickening the rowdy garage-jangle sound and the songwriting reaching for Stones- and Faces-style classic-rock scope. It is looser and warmer than Wild Onion, for listeners who like their bar-band rock young and ragged.
albums.lineage: Builds on Wild Onion's Chicago garage-jangle sound while sounding newly indebted to '70s classic rock.
key_tracks: Walk to the One You Love

albums.label: Bayonet Records
albums.description: Warehouse's second album is a more concise, confident follow-up to Tesseract, keeping the interlocking guitar jams and Elaine Edenfield's fiery frontperson presence. The songs are leaner and more tightly wound, suiting listeners who like angular post-punk with a jangling edge.
albums.lineage: Follows directly from Tesseract's jangling post-punk template, refined after the band's move to Bayonet Records.

albums.label: Domino Recording Co.
albums.description: A genre-hopping record that swings from fiddle-laced country pastiche to noisy skronk to gentle folk within its short, restless tracklist. It's Alex G at his most eclectic, refusing to settle into one style for more than a couple of minutes at a time. It's for listeners who want the fullest picture of his range.
albums.lineage: Broadens the bedroom-pop template of Beach Music with country and folk textures that anticipate his later, more song-oriented Domino albums.

albums.label: Buzz Records
albums.description: Casper Skulls' full-length debut expands their college-radio jangle into bigger, more anthemic arrangements while keeping the dual-vocal chemistry between Melanie St-Pierre and Neil Bednis at the center. The lyrics lean into storytelling and small-scale drama over ringing, layered guitars. It's for fans of R.E.M.-descended Canadian indie rock.
albums.lineage: Follows directly from Lips & Skull on Buzz Records, continuing Toronto's jangle-pop lineage into a fuller studio sound.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: A loose, conversational set of duets and trade-off songs between two of indie rock's most deadpan drawlers, built on unhurried fingerpicked guitar interplay. The two swap verses and harmonize in a way that feels like eavesdropping on old friends. It's for anyone who wants Vile's haze and Barnett's wit in the same room.
albums.lineage: A direct collaboration linking the American slacker-guitar lineage (Vile) with the Australian deadpan-songwriter tradition (Barnett), each feeding the other's fanbase.

albums.label: Captured Tracks
albums.description: A quieter, more acoustic-leaning record built around fingerpicked guitar and synth textures, dealing with DeMarco's relationship with his father. Still slacker in tone but more reflective than his earlier records.
albums.lineage: Shows the slacker-rock lineage bending toward hushed singer-songwriter territory.

albums.label: Good Cheer Records
albums.description: Troper's second album sharpens Beloved's melodic instincts, trading some of the lo-fi scrappiness for slightly cleaner hooks while keeping the rapid-fire, hyper-referential songwriting intact. Short, bright songs pile up quickly, for fans of power pop that never overstays its welcome.
albums.lineage: Continues the GBV-indebted power-pop songwriting of Beloved, tightening the hooks in a way that anticipates Natural Beauty's more melodic turn.
key_tracks: Rock And Roll Will Change The World

albums.label: Grand Jury Music
albums.description: The second half of NE-HI's two-album run, with sharper songwriting and more melodic hooks. The same jangly, fuzz-toned guitar interplay drives it, now with cleaner production and more room to breathe.
albums.lineage: Continuation of NE-HI's jangle/garage-rock songwriting within Chicago's DIY scene.

albums.label: Father Daughter Records
albums.description: A murky, distorted slacker-punk record from a San Francisco band steeped in 90s indie rock, mixing hooky riffs with intentionally lo-fi, gnarled production.
albums.lineage: Descends from Pavement/GBV-style shambling guitar-pop crossed with West Coast noise-punk.

albums.label: Salinas Records
albums.description: Sam Cook-Parrott's project crams scrappy, hook-heavy songs into a short runtime, fuzzy guitars and bright, reedy vocals up front. It keeps the cassette-born intimacy of Something Wild and Torch Song while widening the emotional range.
albums.lineage: Sounds of a piece with the Swearin'/Waxahatchee axis of DIY guitar-pop, sharing its fuzzy, confessional directness.

albums.label: Ivy League Records / Sub Pop
albums.description: Their breakout EP, picked up by Sub Pop for US release, sharpens the interlocking three-guitar jangle of Talk Tight into tighter, more anthemic songs. It is the record that took the band from Melbourne club shows to international festival stages ahead of Hope Downs.
albums.lineage: Bridges Talk Tight's homemade jangle-pop and the fuller, driving sound of Hope Downs, with an interlocking-guitar approach that sounds indebted to the Feelies.

albums.label: Upset the Rhythm / Anti Fade
albums.description: The Melbourne art-punk quartet's second album keeps the terse, sing-song melodies and four-way vocal trades of their debut across punchy, wiry guitar songs. It is wry, hooky punk with a jangling underside, closer to Swell Maps than to hardcore.
albums.lineage: Part of the Melbourne DIY scene around Total Control/UV Race members, extending Terry HQ's terse punk-pop into slightly more orchestrated territory.

albums.label: Merge
albums.description: Produced with John Agnello and her touring band, this is Waxahatchee's loudest, most straightforwardly indie-rock record, about the end of a relationship. It trades the lo-fi hush of her earlier albums for full-band immersion and sharper, angrier hooks.
albums.lineage: The full-band endpoint of Waxahatchee's slacker/DIY period before she moved toward the more countryish Saint Cloud and Tigers Blood.

albums.label: Mom + Pop
albums.description: Lili Trifilio's breakout EP pairs bright, hooky power-pop guitars with plainspoken lyrics about body image and self-doubt, catching viral attention that pushed Beach Bunny from bedroom project to touring band. The songs are short, direct, and instantly catchy. It's for fans of Chicago's guitar-pop scene at its most immediate.
albums.lineage: Grows out of Chicago's DIY guitar-pop scene, sounding kin to acts like Dehd; connects bedroom-pop songwriting to the bigger power-pop sound of the later Blame Game EP.

albums.label: Woodsist
albums.description: A warm, sleepy-eyed sophomore record that became a slow-burn cult favorite, pairing loose, unpolished guitar interplay with plainspoken lyrics about heartbreak and drift. Its patient tempos and conversational vocals put it squarely in the Woodsist label's slacker lineage. It's for fans who want comfort-food indie rock that never raises its voice.
albums.lineage: Continues the band's hushed country-folk sound on the Woodsist label, sounding close to the broader 2010s Kurt Vile/Real Estate axis.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: A full-band re-recording of Toledo's 2011 Bandcamp album, keeping the original's confessional, wordy songwriting about a doomed teenage relationship while giving it a much bigger, more anthemic sound. The original self-released Twin Fantasy holds the same songs in rawer, lo-fi form and is worth hearing alongside it.
albums.lineage: A direct remake of Toledo's own Bandcamp-era masterpiece, connecting his DIY lo-fi songwriting roots to his mature full-band sound.

albums.album: Tell Me How You Really Feel
albums.label: Milk!/Mom+Pop
albums.description: A heavier, more direct record than her debut, with fuzzed-out guitars backing pointed lyrics about self-doubt, sexism, and anger. The production is thicker and the tempos slower, giving her deadpan delivery more room to sting. It's for listeners who want Barnett's wit turned toward something angrier.
albums.lineage: Follows directly from Sometimes I Sit and Think..., sharpening the same slacker-guitar and deadpan-lyric approach into more overtly political territory.

albums.label: Lame-O Records
albums.description: A brief burst of ringing, mid-fi guitar pop from another corner of Lame-O's Philadelphia power-pop stable, all hooks and no filler. Bright, chiming guitars and easy melodies keep it light on its feet. It is a quick hit for fans of short, sweet jangle.
albums.lineage: Sounds akin to the Philadelphia jangle-pop of Hurry and 2nd Grade.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: A sprawling, patient record full of long, meandering songs that stretch his laconic style to its most spacious extreme, including several tracks that pass the nine-minute mark. It trades the tighter pop songwriting of Lotta Sea Lice for hypnotic, repetition-based jams. It's for fans who want to sink into Vile's world for a while rather than get a quick hit.
albums.lineage: Extends the loose, hypnotic guitar-drone side of his songwriting from Smoke Ring for My Halo, sounding indebted to Crazy Horse's long-form jams.

albums.label: Jagjaguwar
albums.description: A slightly more polished, full-band record that keeps Nigel Chapman's signature talk-singing but adds more melodic hooks and confident guitar solos. It is the band's most accessible entry point, warm and ringing without losing its bookish, self-questioning lyrics.
albums.lineage: Third album in Nap Eyes' jangle/talk-song lineage, moving toward a bigger label and wider audience.

albums.label: Father/Daughter
albums.description: A tighter, more anthemic record than the band's early lo-fi releases, mixing power-pop hooks with the same wry, self-aware lyrics. Carmen Perry's bright, direct voice leads punchy, fuzzed guitars built for singing along.
albums.lineage: Continues the Philadelphia DIY-to-power-pop path, sounding of a piece with the later power-pop revival of Lawn and Sharp Pins.

albums.label: Sub Pop
albums.description: Three guitarists trading melodic, chiming lines over motorik rhythms, with plainspoken, road-trip lyrics about growing up and moving on. It is one of the cleanest modern distillations of the Flying Nun/Go-Betweens jangle sound.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Antipodean jangle-pop (The Clean, The Go-Betweens); part of the 2010s Australian guitar-pop wave alongside The Goon Sax and Twerps.

albums.label: Damnably
albums.description: Sun-bleached, reverb-drenched jangle-pop that recalls the Byrds by way of Real Estate. Sumi Choi's calm, plainspoken vocals float over chiming and occasionally surging guitars, for listeners who like their indie rock pristine and wistful.
albums.lineage: Continues Say Sue Me's jangle-pop songwriting, which sounds indebted to Flying Nun and the Byrds.

albums.label: Matador
albums.description: Lindsey Jordan's teenage debut pairs plainspoken, diaristic lyrics with clean, jangly guitar leads that build into big, cathartic choruses. A defining record of the 2010s slacker-rock revival's younger generation.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to 90s and 2000s guitar songwriters like Liz Phair and Rilo Kiley and to the Bandcamp-era DIY scene; it became a touchstone for the wave of young guitar-pop songwriters that followed.

albums.label: Fat Possum Records
albums.description: Sophie Allison's breakout record moves her Bandcamp bedroom-pop into full-band arrangements. It is still built on quiet, confessional verses and 90s-alt-rock-indebted guitar hooks about jealousy and self-doubt.
albums.lineage: Grows out of the Bandcamp/DIY bedroom-pop network and 90s alt-rock guitar songwriting; a borderline case whose pop instincts push toward Context-lane crossover on later records.

albums.label: Carpark Records
albums.description: Sadie Dupuis's band follows Foil Deer by sharpening its knotty, dissonant guitar interplay into more outright pop structures. The hooks are bigger and the tempos brisker, but the lyrics stay confrontational about power and consent, for fans who like their guitar-pop with feedback and bite.
albums.lineage: Continues Speedy Ortiz's noisy, angular guitar-pop lineage from Major Arcana and Foil Deer, tightening the pop hooks without losing the dissonant guitar tangle.

albums.label: Merge Records
albums.description: Swearin's reunion album, its first for Merge, keeps the fuzzed, bittersweet guitar-pop of its Salinas Records releases while sounding fuller and more confident, with Allison Crutchfield and Kyle Gilbride trading songwriting duties as before. Harmonized guitars swing between bright jangle and noisy feedback, for fans of heart-on-sleeve Philadelphia DIY rock.
albums.lineage: A return, after a mid-2010s hiatus, to Swearin's own Philadelphia DIY guitar-pop lineage, a scene it shares with Waxahatchee, the project of Allison Crutchfield's twin sister Katie.

albums.label: Upset the Rhythm / Anti Fade
albums.description: Terry's third LP in three years keeps their formula of terrace-chant choruses and terse, witty verses, alternating scrappy Wire-like guitar scrambles with gentler, synth-shimmered passages. Its lyrics turn a sharper eye on nationalism and colonial history than the earlier records.
albums.lineage: A continuation of the Melbourne post-punk/pop songwriting of Total Control and UV Race's overlapping membership, staying close to Terry HQ's terse jangle-punk template.

albums.label: Slumberland Records
albums.description: Molina brings full-band arrangements back after Confront the Truth's acoustic minimalism, opening with a twelve-string tune that could sit on a Byrds record and closing with gentle, Elliott Smith-like fingerpicking. Nothing is padded; every short song is all melody.
albums.lineage: Splits the difference between Dissed and Dismissed's full-band crunch and Confront the Truth's acoustic intimacy, still sounding rooted in the Byrds/Big Star power-pop seam.

albums.label: Domino Recording Co.
albums.description: A woozy, unsettling record that folds pitch-shifted vocals, folk fingerpicking and eerie electronic textures into some of his most emotionally direct songwriting, circling addiction and loss. Songs like 'Hope' and 'Southern Sky' hold the collage together with plain, aching melodies. It's the most cohesive-feeling statement in Alex G's catalog.
albums.lineage: Builds on the genre-collage approach of Rocket while tightening the emotional focus, setting up the more expansive God Save the Animals.

albums.label: Mac's Record Label
albums.description: Self-released on DeMarco's own label, this record strips his sound to its most repetitive and hypnotic, with simple, mantra-like song structures and titles. A deliberately low-key follow-up that trades hooks for mood.
albums.lineage: DeMarco's move to self-release on his own label echoes the DIY spirit this lane traces.

albums.label: Tiny Engines
albums.description: Truth Club's debut pairs Chris Davis's conversational, self-lacerating lyrics with tense, angular guitar interplay that snaps between quiet verses and squalling choruses. It sounds like a Raleigh house-show band that grew up on Pavement and Cap'n Jazz in equal measure. Good for listeners who want their slacker rock a little more wound-up and anxious.
albums.lineage: Grows out of the Pavement/GBV lineage of loud-quiet indie rock filtered through Raleigh's DIY basement scene; feeds directly into the tighter, more melodic songwriting of Running From the Chase.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A warmer, more classic-rock-leaning record that rounds out the band's transition from scrappy garage kids to accomplished songwriters. Piano, harmonies and relaxed grooves replace much of the old rowdiness, for fans of easygoing '70s-style rock.
albums.lineage: Later-period Twin Peaks, still rooted in the band's Chicago garage-jangle scene origins.

albums.label: Double Double Whammy
albums.description: Peter Gill's debut as 2nd Grade crams hook after hook into a scrappy, GBV-scaled power-pop sprawl, rarely settling into one idea for more than two minutes. It set the template for the project's compulsively prolific, miniature-song aesthetic.
albums.lineage: Sounds directly descended from Guided by Voices' song-fragment power pop, and comes out of the same Philadelphia scene as Hurry and Golden Apples.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: A deliberately polarizing pivot toward synths, drum machines and EDM-adjacent production, while keeping Toledo's anxious, funny-sad lyricism intact. It traded the noisy guitar rock of Teens of Denial for something colder and more electronic. It's for fans willing to follow the band away from its guitar-rock comfort zone.
albums.lineage: A deliberate break from the Crazy Horse and jangle-rock guitar sound of Teens of Denial, showing the DIY-to-major-indie pipeline can still take creative risks.

albums.label: You've Changed Records
albums.description: Written in response to ghostly samples McKiel found on a used reel-to-reel tape, this record blends hushed, fingerpicked songwriting with warped found-sound textures into something inventive and haunting. It's a quieter, more experimental turn than straightforward jangle-pop but keeps a strong melodic core. It's for fans of Canadian DIY songwriting with a spectral edge.
albums.lineage: Part of the You've Changed Records roster connecting Maritime Canada's indie scene to the wider lo-fi/jangle underground; feeds into Hex's continued collaboration with Jay Crocker.

albums.label: Mint Records
albums.description: Kiwi Jr.'s debut full-length sets the template the band would refine on later Sub Pop records: chiming, Pavement-indebted guitar lines, deadpan sing-speak vocals, and lyrics stuffed with dry pop-culture asides. It's rougher around the edges than Cooler Returns but already has the band's melodic hooks in place. It's for fans who want the origin point of their jangle-pop run.
albums.lineage: Grows out of Toronto's DIY guitar-pop scene and the Pavement/Guided by Voices lineage; set up the band's jump to Sub Pop for Cooler Returns and Chopper.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Lawn's second album expands on the duo's breezy power-pop hooks across unhurried songs, with a relaxed, roomy sound ahead of the tighter Bigger Sprout. It's a warmer, looser record than what came before or after, for fans of easygoing guitar pop.
albums.lineage: Sits between Lawn's earlier, more post-punk-tinged material and the tighter power pop of Bigger Sprout and God Made The Highway.

albums.label: Tender Loving Empire
albums.description: Troper's third album swaps the earlier records' snottiness for plainer, more durable storytelling, anchored by the Kinks-indebted 'Jas From Australia'. Clean, chiming guitars and sweeter melodies make it his most approachable record, for fans of classic power-pop craft.
albums.lineage: A more melodically direct turn from Troper's earlier GBV-style scrappiness, sounding closer to the Kinks and Teenage Fanclub end of the power-pop lineage.

albums.label: Royal Mountain Records
albums.description: Nap Eyes' most direct, hook-forward record, still built on Chapman's conversational delivery but with brighter, more confident arrangements.
albums.lineage: Continues the band's jangle/talk-song lineage into a fourth album.

albums.label: Sub Pop
albums.description: A sunnier, more confident sequel to Hope Downs, with the same three-guitar interlock but bigger choruses and warmer production. Written partly about touring and homesickness.
albums.lineage: Sounds like second-generation Flying Nun-indebted jangle-pop, continuing the band's refinement of the sound.

albums.label: Winspear
albums.description: Slow Pulp's debut full-length was finished amid health crises and a pandemic, blending blown-out shoegaze guitar with unusually direct, hooky songwriting. It channels the band's explosive live intensity into a more controlled studio record.
albums.lineage: Grows out of Slow Pulp's Chicago/Madison shoegaze-pop beginnings, a lighter, poppier cousin to Wednesday's countrygaze template.

albums.label: Mom + Pop
albums.description: A tighter, more polished EP than Prom Queen, with Beach Bunny's power-pop hooks pushed toward arena-ready choruses while the lyrics stay pointed and personal. It followed their first full-length and shows the band's most immediate, radio-ready songwriting.
albums.lineage: Continues the Chicago guitar-pop lineage of Prom Queen, sharpening the hooks as the band's audience grew.

albums.label: Buzz Records
albums.description: A more confident, dynamically varied record than their debut, still anchored by ringing guitar interplay and dual-vocal storytelling but pushing into denser arrangements and darker lyrical territory. It's the sound of a band settling comfortably into its own identity within Toronto's jangle-pop scene. It's for fans who followed the band from their Buzz Records beginnings.
albums.lineage: The most developed entry in Casper Skulls' Buzz Records run, later followed by Kit-Cat on Next Door Records.

albums.label: Milk! Records
albums.description: A calmer record that trades some of Barnett's wordplay density for spacious, drum-machine-inflected slacker pop. Hushed, breezy arrangements suit its themes of patience and care.
albums.lineage: Barnett's songwriting, which sounds indebted to Pavement, softened toward indie-pop.

albums.label: Carpark Records
albums.description: Ducks Ltd.'s debut full-length sets the duo's template of chiming, propulsive guitar interplay over brisk rhythms, drawing on '80s college-rock jangle filtered through a modern anxious lyric sheet. Tom McGreevy's plainspoken vocals ride on top of Evan Lewis's careening guitar lines. It's for fans of Sarah Records-style jangle brought into the present.
albums.lineage: Comes out of the Toronto DIY scene and sounds indebted to the Flying Nun/Go-Betweens jangle-pop lineage; set up Harm's Way's fuller studio sound.

albums.label: Grand Jury Music
albums.description: Charlie Martin and Will Taylor's duo makes soft-focus, mid-fi slacker pop, warm and unhurried. Plain-spoken affection rides gentle drum-machine pulses and hushed, lullaby-like vocals, for listeners who want indie rock as a quiet comfort.
albums.lineage: Sounds descended from the lo-fi college-radio-to-Bandcamp lineage of Duster and Alex G.

albums.label: Lame-O Records
albums.description: Matt Scottoline's project turns plainspoken heartbreak into tight, hook-forward power pop recorded with an easy, unfussy jangle. It sits alongside Philadelphia's current power-pop revival, for fans of short, sweet, sad songs.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Big Star and Superchunk, filtered through the Philadelphia DIY scene.

albums.label: Sub Pop
albums.description: Toronto's Kiwi Jr. sharpen their Pavement- and GBV-descended jangle into a wry, hooky second album. Deadpan vocals trade in pop-culture references and small stories over bright, clipped guitars.
albums.lineage: Sounds directly indebted to Pavement and Guided by Voices.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A cohesive, jittery-warm record of jangle-pop songwriting from a Grand Rapids band. It mixes heavy rock'n'roll textures with pop hooks, built to be heard as a full album.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Big Star/Flying Nun jangle-pop songwriting by way of the Midwest DIY circuit.

albums.label: Bar/None Records
albums.description: A tighter, more melodic version of Pardoner's slacker-punk sound, still caked in fuzz but with clearer hooks poking through the murk. Fast, messy guitars and yelped vocals make it for listeners who like their indie rock loud and a little unhinged.
albums.lineage: Continuation of Pardoner's Pavement/GBV-descended noisy slacker-pop songwriting.

albums.label: Father/Daughter Records
albums.description: Remember Sports' third Father/Daughter album builds on Slow Buzz's expanded arrangements, with the four members trading instruments and adding synths and drum machines to the guitar-pop core. Carmen Perry sings her sharpest lyrics yet about self-forgiveness, for listeners who like power pop with rough edges.
albums.lineage: The most ambitious entry in Remember Sports' arc from scrappy basement pop-punk (All of Something) toward richly arranged power pop.

albums.label: Matador
albums.description: A more produced, emotionally raw follow-up to Lush, adding synths and string arrangements to Jordan's core jangle-guitar sound. Her voice pushes into more theatrical territory, for listeners who want the heartbreak bigger and glossier.
albums.lineage: Second chapter of Snail Mail's slacker-to-art-pop evolution.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: The Brisbane trio add synths and sheen to their jangle-pop, its three songwriters trading plainspoken, bittersweet verses. Close harmonies and deadpan delivery keep it wry and tender.
albums.lineage: Founding member Louis Forster is the son of the Go-Betweens' Robert Forster; the band's jangle sounds descended from the Go-Betweens and Flying Nun.

albums.label: Double Double Whammy
albums.description: 2nd Grade's second album keeps the compulsive hook-density of Hit to Hit but tightens the songwriting, with titles nodding to Keith Richards and Rolling Stone covers. Sixteen songs of unpretentious, Big Star-scaled jangle-pop.
albums.lineage: Continues Peter Gill's GBV-indebted power-pop songwriting, part of Philadelphia's power-pop revival alongside Hurry.

albums.label: Domino Recording Company
albums.description: Alex Giannascoli's album pairs pitched-up vocal tics and Auto-Tune warps with plainspoken, sometimes menacing songwriting about faith and small-town life. Gentle acoustic arrangements and gospel-tinged hooks sit next to eerie, lo-fi textures. It suits listeners who like songs that are tender and unsettling at once.
albums.lineage: Grew out of Bandcamp-era home recording; its fragmentary lo-fi songcraft sounds indebted to Guided by Voices and Elliott Smith.

albums.label: Lame-O Records
albums.description: James Goodson's project crams huge hooks into no-second-wasted power pop, like Fountains of Wayne played at ear-shattering volume. Crazy Horse-style fuzz and anthemic choruses fill short, breathless songs.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Big Star and Fountains of Wayne melodicism, blown out with fuzz-pedal DIY energy.

albums.album: If You Knew Would You Believe It?
albums.label: Smoking Room
albums.description: A guitar-forward home-recorded record with hooky choruses that slides between snotty rock, stargazing psych, and introspective folk, part of Graham Hunt's prolific self-released catalog out of Madison, Wisconsin. It leans on a '90s alt-rock sensibility while still sounding distinctly homemade. It's for fans of one-person bedroom rock records with real songwriting range.
albums.lineage: Part of Hunt's ongoing self-released Bandcamp catalog that runs from lo-fi power pop through to the more studio-polished American Pyramid.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: Three young Chicagoans' debut is an efficient romp through indie rock's post-punk and jangle fringes. Interlocking guitars, feedback, and deadpan vocals keep songs short and sharp. It suits listeners who love noisy, tasteful '90s-style indie rock.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Pavement and Sonic Youth's guitar interplay, filtered through Chicago's all-ages DIY scene.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Joe Glass's debut showcases his knack for an airtight hook across slightly twangy, ramshackle rockers pulling from Nuggets-style garage pop and '90s indie rock. It's scrappy and fast, for fans of the current Midwestern power-pop underground.
albums.lineage: Sounds of a piece with the Chicago-area DIY power-pop underground around Lifeguard and Sharp Pins, sharing their Nuggets-inspired hooks.

albums.label: Sub Pop
albums.description: Kiwi Jr.'s third album adds synths and sheen to their wit-and-melody formula, sardonic Toronto indie rock that balances humor and hooks. It builds on the jangle of Cooler Returns and Football Money with a glossier, more synth-lit sound.
albums.lineage: Continues the band's jangle, which sounds descended from Pavement and GBV.

albums.label: Verve Records
albums.description: Vile's first album after leaving Matador for Verve leans further into home-studio synth textures and drum-machine pulses while keeping his familiar mumbled melodies intact. It's looser and more playful than his 2010s work, closer to a solo bedroom record again, for longtime fans curious how his sound kept drifting.
albums.lineage: A return to the DIY, self-produced instincts of his earliest lo-fi tapes, now filtered through two decades of studio experience.

albums.label: Born Yesterday Records
albums.description: A New Orleans duo splitting the difference between breezy power-pop hooks and nervy post-punk edges, with trading vocals and taut, bright guitars. It sits in the same power-pop revival as Dazy, 2nd Grade and Mo Troper.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to the Big Star power-pop line crossed with post-punk tension, part of the mid-2020s power-pop revival.

albums.label: Lame-O Records
albums.description: Fifteen hook-dense power-pop tracks from a Portland songwriter, pairing clever, self-aware writing with warmth and classic melodies. Troper's own tagline calls his style 'the Conker's Bad Fur Day of power pop,' which captures its mix of nerdy reference and sugar rush.
albums.lineage: Direct descendant of the Big Star/Teenage Fanclub power-pop lineage, part of the 2020s power-pop revival alongside Sharp Pins and Lawn.

albums.label: Sub Pop
albums.description: A darker, more expansive record with longer song structures and heavier guitar tones layered under the band's signature three-guitar jangle. It is the band's most textured album, for listeners who want the chime with more shadow.
albums.lineage: Shows the band stretching its Flying Nun-indebted jangle sound toward denser, more textured arrangements.

albums.label: Damnably
albums.description: Say Sue Me's most inward record is built around themes of self-love and realization rather than the surf-jangle bounce of earlier singles. Slower tempos and softer arrangements widen the palette without losing the Busan band's pristine, throwback jangle-pop core.
albums.lineage: Continues the Busan band's pristine throwback indie-pop, which sounds close to Alvvays, turning inward after Where We Were Together.

albums.label: Carpark Records
albums.description: Elizabeth Stokes writes tight, guitar-heavy songs that read as character studies of relationships' aftermaths. Harmonized guitars and anthemic choruses give the heartbreak a bright, driving lift.
albums.lineage: Sounds akin to the New Zealand jangle-pop tradition around Flying Nun, crossed with American power pop.

albums.label: Bingo Records
albums.description: The Welsh duo's debut album packs deceptively simple garage-pop melodies into a scrappy, ramshackle energy, with the pair's back-and-forth deadpan vocals doing most of the heavy lifting. Songs whip by quickly, favoring hooks over polish. It's the record that set up their prolific run before Sub Pop signed them.
albums.lineage: Sounds of a piece with the UK DIY garage-pop underground that runs parallel to the American slacker/jangle revival; the band later signed to Sub Pop.

albums.label: Keeled Scales
albums.description: Why Bonnie's debut full-length trades their earlier bedroom dream pop for raw-edged, feedback-streaked indie rock with a Texas twang in the melodies. Blair Howerton's clear, unhurried voice rides over fuzzy guitars and road-trip imagery. It suits listeners who like their '90s-style alt-rock with a hint of country dust.
albums.lineage: A Texas band's move from dream pop toward a more country-and-alt-rock-inflected sound, resembling the wider indie-twang turn without being a straight country record.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: An early record mixing jangly guitar with drum machines and synths in an off-kilter, homemade pop style. It feels like a bedroom experiment in progress, for listeners who enjoy lo-fi indie rock that wanders.
albums.lineage: Part of the DIY/Bandcamp jangle-pop network this lane traces from Flying Nun and college radio.

albums.label: ANTI-
albums.description: Detroit's Bonny Doon make their ANTI- debut breezier and more accessible than past records, with lyrics that sneak up on the listener over unhurried, conversational arrangements. Close harmonies and hushed, deadpan vocals keep it gentle.
albums.lineage: Slacker-folk that sounds indebted to the Silver Jews and Palace, filtered through Detroit's indie scene.

albums.label: Bar/None Records
albums.description: Blue Broderick's Diners project goes full power-pop on this breezy guitar-pop record, with clear DNA from Tom Petty, Big Star and Fountains of Wayne. Every song is built for maximum hum-along appeal, bright guitars and stacked harmonies up front. It's for fans who want classic power-pop songcraft filtered through a bedroom-pop sensibility.
albums.lineage: Moves Broderick's earlier lo-fi Diners records toward the wider power-pop revival, sounding indebted to Petty, Big Star and Fountains of Wayne.

albums.label: Lame-O Records
albums.description: Golden Apples' hookiest, most fuzzed-out set is packed with memorable choruses in the power-pop and jangle vein. Distorted guitars and bright melodies push the songs forward without losing their homemade Philadelphia feel.
albums.lineage: Big Star melodicism via Philadelphia's power-pop revival.

albums.label: Smoking Room
albums.description: A self-released Wisconsin power-pop record with effortless hooks and a '90s rock sensibility, continuing Graham Hunt's steady run of home-recorded guitar-pop albums. The songwriting is direct and unfussy, favoring melody over studio polish. It's for fans who want deep-catalog power pop from outside the usual coastal scenes.
albums.lineage: Sits between If You Knew Would You Believe It? and Timeless World Forever in Hunt's self-released discography.

albums.label: Third Man Records
albums.description: Will Anderson's project buries plainspoken, slacker-jangly songwriting under warm shoegaze fuzz and feedback. Cartwheel was his Third Man Records debut, for listeners who like hooks hidden inside a noise wall.
albums.lineage: Sits between shoegaze fuzz and the jangle-pop tradition, sounding indebted to Guided by Voices' song-fragment economy.

albums.label: Sub Pop Records
albums.description: A dreamier, more polished turn for the garage-glam lifer Kyle Thomas, trading his usual fuzzed-out riffs for jangly, synth-dusted power pop with a wide-eyed, sun-drenched feel. It's a gentler record than his 2010s output but keeps his knack for an instant hook. It's for fans who like their power pop with a cosmic-country glow.
albums.lineage: King Tuff's catalog runs from 2000s garage-punk through Sub Pop glam-rock; Smalltown Stardust pulls him into the same jangly, twang-adjacent revival as his 2010s peers.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: The Upper Peninsula band's self-titled album crams dense, hooky songs into a very short runtime, sounding indebted to Fountains of Wayne, PUP and Rozwell Kid in equal measure. It is power pop with a Midwestern punk snap, over almost before it starts.
albums.lineage: A Marquette, Michigan strain of pop-punk-inflected power pop, indebted to Fountains of Wayne's hook density and 1990s Midwest punk energy.

albums.label: Mac's Record Label
albums.description: A wordless, tape-warped song cycle Mac DeMarco pieced together while driving cross-country, all warm Rhodes, brushed drums and looping guitar vamps instead of his usual slack-jawed vocals. It plays like a private travelogue, mixing his usual chorus-pedal haze with lounge and ambient touches. For listeners who want the DeMarco sound stripped of singing.
albums.lineage: Extends the bedroom-pop haze of his Captured Tracks records into instrumental territory, closer to Jim O'Rourke's ambient side than to Pavement.

albums.label: Hallogallo Tapes
albums.description: Kai Slater's (Lifeguard, Dwaal Troupe) solo power-pop project delivers bedroom-recorded, Big Star/Teenage Fanclub-style hooks. Short, jangly songs come wrapped in scrappy tape-hiss charm, for listeners who like their power pop homemade.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to the Big Star power-pop lineage by way of lo-fi, self-recorded bedroom pop.

albums.label: ANTI-
albums.description: Slow Pulp's second album warms its shoegaze-scale guitars with Americana hues, slide and acoustic textures, and pristine pop hooks without any filler. It's their most confident synthesis of noise and twang.
albums.lineage: Extends Moveys' shoegaze-pop into more overtly Americana-tinged territory, sounding close to the countrygaze lineage of Wednesday and Great Grandpa.

albums.label: Wax Nine Records
albums.description: Speedy Ortiz's fourth album pushes the band's gnarled guitar interplay toward a vast, heavier sound, with long solos and walls of feedback. Sadie Dupuis's lyrics confront trauma and music-industry hypocrisy, making it the band's most expansive and pointed record.
albums.lineage: The most expansive entry in Speedy Ortiz's noisy indie-rock lineage from Major Arcana onward, still rooted in the same angular guitar tangle.

albums.label: Lame-O Records
albums.description: Superviolet's debut is buoyant, hook-forward power pop full of bright, jangling guitars and warm, earnest vocals. Its unfussy songs read as a career-best distillation of that songwriting style, for fans of sunny, melodic guitar pop.
albums.lineage: A Columbus, Ohio power-pop project in the Teenage Fanclub/Superchunk lineage, part of the same 2020s power-pop revival as Sharp Pins and Hurry.

albums.label: Upset the Rhythm / Anti Fade
albums.description: Five years on from I'm Terry, the band's fourth album dresses their terse four-vocal punk-pop in fuller production while lyrically taking aim at Australia's colonial history. The detuned, scrappy guitars and chant-along choruses are still at the core, for fans of wry, political post-punk.
albums.lineage: A late-period expansion of the same Melbourne art-punk lineage, sharing members with Total Control and UV Race, that produced Terry HQ.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A sprawling, hour-long set of relentlessly catchy, fuzz-wrapped garage pop with great dual-singer chemistry. Most songs are short and rowdy, stacking jokes and hooks at speed.
albums.lineage: Continues the band's garage sound, which sounds indebted to Nuggets, at maximalist length.

albums.label: Trouble in Mind
albums.description: A Welsh band's debut applies ringing, Byrds/Feelies-style jangle guitar to raw, personal songwriting about grief and family, one of the sharpest post-2020s jangle-revival records.
albums.lineage: Direct descendant of classic jangle-pop (The Feelies, early R.E.M., Flying Nun bands).

albums.label: Double Double Whammy
albums.description: A more confident, widescreen version of the Truth Club sound, moving from hushed confession to full-band catharsis with a voice that cracks at the edges of big, hooky choruses. It plays like a document of getting older and more self-aware without losing any of the tension of the debut.
albums.lineage: Continues Truth Club's basement-scene, Pavement/GBV-descended jangle-and-noise songwriting into a more polished, emotionally direct register.

albums.label: Winspear
albums.description: A New Orleans duo's fourth LP moves away from disco nostalgia toward more personal, unselfconscious songwriting. Its effortless-sounding hooks and smooth pop craft recall Steely Dan and the Beach Boys.
albums.lineage: Descends from breezy 70s pop-rock songwriting filtered through 2010s New Orleans indie pop.

albums.label: Double Double Whammy
albums.description: 2nd Grade's third full-length is its most expansive yet, still built from the same rapid-fire jangling hooks and wry titles as its predecessors. It is Peter Gill's project at its most prolific and melodically confident, for fans who like their power pop in short, bright bursts.
albums.lineage: The latest entry in 2nd Grade's GBV/Big Star-indebted-sounding power-pop project, part of Philadelphia's mid-2020s jangle-pop scene.

albums.label: Carpark Records
albums.description: Ducks Ltd.'s most fleshed-out record is precise and propulsive jangle-pop with careening riffs and power-pop melodies. Bright guitars and a fuller band sound frame the duo's anxious, plainspoken lyrics. It's the fullest realization yet of their college-rock-meets-anxiety songwriting.
albums.lineage: Builds on Modern Fiction's jangle foundation with a bigger, more collaborative studio sound.

albums.label: Tiny Engines
albums.description: An early-2024 power-pop full-length released on the emo/indie label Tiny Engines, part of a wave of DIY guitar-pop records flagged in Josh Terry's most-anticipated list that year. Details on its sound are limited, but its label and placement put it squarely in the jangle/power-pop underground. It's a deep-cut pick for listeners exploring Tiny Engines' current roster.
albums.lineage: Released on Tiny Engines, a label historically associated with emo and twangy emo crossovers, connecting it to the C9 emo-crossover lane as well as straight power pop.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: This Columbus power trio's three-song EP is pummeling, loud and varied, with each track sounding markedly different but united by an animated heaviness. It's a live-wire document of a genuinely ferocious band, for fans of noisy Midwestern guitar rock that hits hard in short bursts.
albums.lineage: Sounds of a piece with the current Midwest DIY noise-rock underground where it overlaps with the slacker/jangle scene at its loudest edge.

albums.label: Arts & Crafts
albums.description: A long, double-LP-length set with stronger melodies and more hi-fi recording than earlier Hovvdy work. Hushed, lullaby-soft vocals and gentle pulses keep the duo's intimacy intact even as the sound fills out.
albums.lineage: Continues Hovvdy's lo-fi slacker-pop arc toward fuller production.

albums.label: You've Changed Records
albums.description: A second collaboration with producer Jay Crocker, this record folds more synths and studio texture into McKiel's hushed songwriting without losing the strange, homemade intimacy of Bobby Joe Hope. Murmured vocals sit inside warm, slightly warped arrangements. It's for fans of understated, atmosphere-first Canadian indie rock.
albums.lineage: Continues the Crocker/McKiel partnership begun on Bobby Joe Hope, part of the same You've Changed Records lineage.

albums.label: Winspear
albums.description: Grand Rapids trio Major Murphy follows Access with a warm, psychedelic-tinged set that weaves classic-rock and vintage soft-rock touches into their usual blend of 1990s indie looseness and 1970s AM-radio warmth. It's an emotionally direct record, for listeners who like their guitar pop mellow and melodic.
albums.lineage: Extends Major Murphy's own hybrid of 1990s indie rock and 1970s soft-rock songwriting established on Access, sounding indebted to Big Star's more orchestrated moments.

albums.label: You've Changed Records
albums.description: The band pairs its conversational, bookish lyrics with sunny organ and strong, ringing guitar work. Nigel Chapman's half-spoken delivery stays at the center, making it a warm late-career entry for fans of talky, unhurried guitar rock.
albums.lineage: Latest chapter in Nap Eyes' jangle songwriting, which sounds indebted to Silver Jews and the Velvet Underground.

albums.label: Carpark Records
albums.description: Rui Gabriel's solo debut uses a light palette of fun grooves and Summerteeth-grade hooks to write self-aware songs about class and miscommunication. It is bright, sing-along power pop for listeners who like wry lyrics over tuneful, loose-limbed studio pop.
albums.lineage: A solo power-pop outlet that sounds indebted to Wilco's Summerteeth-era studio pop.

albums.album: On the Intricate Inner Workings of the System
albums.label: Sub Pop
albums.description: The Welsh band's Sub Pop debut is Modern Lovers-meets-Nuggets garage rock with sarcastic dual vocals and clanging riffs. Songs are short, rowdy and funny-sad, often done in under two minutes.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Nuggets garage and the talky deadpan of Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers.

albums.album: Box for Buddy, Box for Star
albums.label: Double Double Whammy
albums.description: Nate Amos's (Water From Your Eyes) solo project delivers warped, hooky pop songs that recall the Postal Service, Big Star and the Magnetic Fields. Drum machines and home-recorded synths sit under genuine power-pop songwriting, sweet and slightly off-kilter.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Big Star power-pop songwriting, filtered through home-recorded, synth-augmented indie pop.
key_tracks: Box for Buddy, Box for Star

albums.label: Winspear
albums.description: Indiana songwriters Kevin Krauter and Nina Pitchkites blend shoegaze haze, grunge fuzz and power-pop hooks on their debut LP. It moves between pillowy atmospherics and scathing distortion, for fans of melodic, loud '90s-style guitar rock.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to the Big Star power-pop line crossed with 90s alt-rock guitar tones.

albums.label: Shuga Records
albums.description: Twin Peaks' Cadien Lake James steps out solo here, trading his main band's raw garage-pop for glimmering, tastefully electronic jangle-pop. It is a more polished, atmospheric record than his band's work, for listeners who like breezy guitar-pop with soft synth shading.
albums.lineage: A solo offshoot of Twin Peaks' garage-jangle songwriting, filtered through cleaner electronic production.

albums.label: RCA Records
albums.description: Alex G's major-label debut keeps his warped, intimate production but pushes toward higher fidelity. Latter-day R.E.M. and Daniel Johnston echoes are folded into the same gentle-menace songwriting that runs through his earlier records, with the title track 'Headlights' as the clearest example.
albums.lineage: Continues Alex G's arc from Bandcamp lo-fi into a wider, still jangle-rooted indie-pop palette.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Chicago songwriter Ben Astrachan's solo debut is maximalist and ambitious, packing its songs with wailing guitars and a multitude of '60s-and-'70s-indebted melodic twists. It's conceptual rock music delivered in an off-kilter, deliriously infectious way rather than as straight pastiche. It's for fans of Chicago's current crop of detail-obsessed guitar-pop songwriters.
albums.lineage: Sounds of a piece with Chicago acts like Smushie and Shoulderbird, connecting classic-rock revivalism to the current power-pop/jangle underground.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: A concept album set at a fictional university, this record returns Car Seat Headrest to a bigger, more guitar-driven full-band sound after the electronic detour of Making a Door Less Open. Toledo's wordy, theatrical songwriting is at its most ambitious here, built around a cast of recurring characters. It's for longtime fans who wanted the band's rock muscle back.
albums.lineage: A return to the anthemic guitar-rock lineage of Teens of Denial after the band's synth-pop experiment, keeping Toledo's literary songwriting intact.

albums.label: Seasick Records
albums.description: Loud, relentlessly hooky rock that channels Summerteeth-era Wilco and Ty Segall's frantic energy. Crazy Horse fuzz and Telecaster twang back small-town storytelling at full tilt.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Neil Young & Crazy Horse fuzz, with Wilco's Americana-pop as a touchstone.

albums.label: Next Door Records
albums.description: Casper Skulls' latest LP has the dual-vocal chemistry and college-radio jangle of a band drawing on Pavement, R.E.M. and Superchunk, full of lived-in warmth. Guitars ring and interlock while the vocal trade-offs keep the songs feeling conversational. It's for longtime fans of the band's steady evolution.
albums.lineage: Continues the jangle-pop lineage established on Buzz Records, now on Next Door Records with a warmer, more assured sound.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Cult New York duo Frog's latest album is folky, lo-fi and scrappy, like Modest Mouse playing Pinegrove-style heart-on-sleeve songs. A piano-led opener and banjo-anchored tracks wrap aching lyrics in charmingly unadorned production. It's for fans who want deadpan, funny-sad songwriting without any studio gloss.
albums.lineage: A long-running New York DIY act that sounds indebted to Drag City-style funny-sad songwriting, filtered through the lo-fi Bandcamp underground.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Russell Edling's group turns its own songwriting process inside out across a spacious, nervy set of fuzzed and jangling power pop. Dreamy mellotron cuts against scrubby guitars, with a playful, Elephant 6-style looseness.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Big Star and Elephant 6 melodicism, sitting within Philadelphia's current power-pop scene.
key_tracks: Another Grand Offering for the Swine

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Adventurous, stylistically shifting indie rock that still flows front to back, with Built to Spill and Pavement echoes throughout. Jangling guitars stretch into long solos beneath deadpan vocals.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Pavement's loose song-suite structure and Built to Spill's guitar interplay.

albums.label: Rotten Apple
albums.description: A twee-punk-leaning collection of home recordings, full of pristine, thoughtful jangle-pop with big hooks and surging punk energy. Lo-fi fidelity and short songs keep it scrappy and small-town intimate.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Guided by Voices and Beat Happening's DIY-jangle lineage.

albums.label: Run For Cover Records
albums.description: Another entry in Graham Hunt's prolific self-released catalog, continuing his blend of hooky, home-recorded power pop with wide-ranging classic-rock and psych touches. Bright guitars and direct melodies keep it unfussy, for listeners tracking his steady, low-key discography.
albums.lineage: Part of Hunt's ongoing solo catalog that runs directly into American Pyramid's bigger studio sound.

albums.label: Matador Records
albums.description: A more direct second album of ramshackle, perfect pop songs, with grooves and glowing harmonies replacing the debut's noisier fringes. Clean, jangling guitars and deadpan vocals keep the songs short and spare.
albums.lineage: Continues Horsegirl's post-punk and jangle sound, akin to Pavement, toward cleaner pop songwriting.

albums.label: Exploding In Sound Records
albums.description: Lawn's most confident record yet, a scrappy blend of post-punk and power-pop with dual lead vocals trading off across hook-heavy songs. It is a punchy distillation of the New Orleans band's sound, wiry guitars and all.
albums.lineage: Continues Lawn's power-pop/post-punk hybrid songwriting into a bigger, punchier register.

albums.label: Mac's Record Label
albums.description: Mac DeMarco's Guitar returns to vocal pop songwriting after the instrumental detour of Five Easy Hot Dogs, foregrounding warm guitar tone and his familiar half-mumbled melodies. It is unhurried, private-sounding pop built for headphones on a walk. Fans of Salad Days will find the same loose, wobbly charm.
albums.lineage: A return to the vocal jangle-pop songwriting of Salad Days and This Old Dog after an instrumental record, still rooted in his Captured Tracks-era slacker sound.

albums.label: Earth Libraries
albums.description: A warm, crisp midtempo jangle record built around layered melodies and unvarnished lyricism, with pedal steel coloring several tracks. It stakes out its own lane of graceful, inviting jangle-pop for listeners who like their guitar pop gentle.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to the DIY jangle/college-radio line (Big Star, Flying Nun), filtered through 2020s Midwest indie rock.

albums.label: K Records / Perennial
albums.description: A sprawling set from Kai Slater, packed with 1965-styled jangle hooks and bright, trebly guitars. It is the most maximalist Sharp Pins record yet, stringing together short, hook-forward pop songs with barely a pause between them.
albums.lineage: Extends Sharp Pins' Nuggets/Big Star-sounding jangle-pop into a longer, more song-crammed format, released through K Records and Perennial.

albums.label: K Records / Perennial
albums.description: Kai Slater's Sharp Pins project follows Turtle Rock with fourteen driving, Nuggets-indebted power-pop songs, tighter and more melodically direct than before. Calvin Johnson's K Records/Perennial imprint released it, cementing Sharp Pins' place in the Big Star-to-GBV jangle-pop lineage.
albums.lineage: Follows Turtle Rock in the 1960s-garage-into-Big-Star jangle-pop lineage; its release through K Records/Perennial places it in a long-running indie-pop label network.

albums.label: Third Man Records
albums.description: This sophomore LP from Melbourne's the Belair Lip Bombs is frenetic, interlocking power pop fronted by the commanding Maisie Everett. The guitars careen and lock together in a way that recalls Australia's jangle-rock lineage while the choruses aim straight for arenas, for fans of big, direct guitar pop.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Melbourne's interlocking-guitar jangle rock in the Rolling Blackouts C.F. mold, now on Third Man Records' power-pop and garage-rock roster.
key_tracks: Don't Let Them Tell You (It's Fair)

albums.label: Sub Pop Records
albums.description: The Bug Club's second Sub Pop record streamlines their oddball garage-pop into catchier, tighter songs, with the jokes landing harder and the choruses stickier than ever. The dual vocals of Sam Willmett and Tilly Harris trade lines with an easy chemistry throughout. It's for listeners who want slacker-pop songwriting that's actually secretly very well-crafted.
albums.lineage: Continues the band's garage-punk-to-power-pop evolution begun on Green Dream in F#, now filtered through a major indie label's reach.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: New Orleans slacker-pop trio The Convenience deliver thirteen loose, deadpan-sung tracks built on jangling, lightly lo-fi guitars. The songwriting is plainspoken and wry, closer to a conversation than a performance, in the same Crescent City DIY scene as Lawn.
albums.lineage: Part of New Orleans' current jangle/slacker cluster alongside Lawn.
key_tracks: I Got Exactly What I Wanted

albums.label: Trouble in Mind
albums.description: A follow-up that keeps The Tubs' chiming jangle-pop core while broadening the arrangements. It continues the band's run of sharply written, classic-sounding guitar-pop, with bright leads and a dry, baritone lead voice.
albums.lineage: Continues The Tubs' jangle-pop, which sounds indebted to '80s British and Antipodean guitar pop.

albums.label: Double Double Whammy
albums.description: Nate Amos (also of Water From Your Eyes) re-recorded songs from across his sprawling This Is Lorelei back catalog, tracked quickly to keep the straight-to-Bandcamp spirit of the originals. It works as a breezy, guitar-pop-facing entry point to his catalog rather than a best-of.
albums.lineage: A deliberate reconnection to Amos's earlier lo-fi Bandcamp songwriting, following Box for Buddy, Box for Star.

albums.label: Self-released
